rv.q: Something is inevitably lost in adapting the material for a modern audience that has outgrown its fear and awe of hellfire and damnation.
By the end, despite Jacobs-Jenkins’s tricks and Neugebauer’s staging savvy — this is another perfectly rendered production from the director of The Wolves
Stranded between cosmic earnestness and a collegiate urge to interrogate weird old texts, Everybody has trouble holding onto a fixed identity.
Here, though, such self-consciousness curdles, despite some amusing “who’s on first”-style circular dialogue on weighty subjects like the existence of God.
For all its artistic ambitions, Everybody turns out to be confusing and disjointed, filled with stylistic diversions that more often than not prove underwhelming.
The show, on the other hand, is sophomoric nonsense and quickly wears out its welcome.
There is nothing preachy or sententious about the text or Lila Neugebauer's delightful production.
My dears, you have much to look forward to.
As it turned out, Jacobs-Jenkins and his Everybody is very good indeed.
Everybody is ambitious and overstuffed, bristling with both ideas and narrative experiments.
“Everybody” is 90 minutes of theatrical whimsy, and it’s remarkable that Jacobs-Jenkins’s wit and invention flag only at the very end...

In director Lila Neugebauer's slick and irreverent production, Jacobs-Jenkins seems more content with riffing on old-time religion by replacing the fear of God with the humorous acceptance of life's disappointments.
It gives the play an impromptu, seat-of-the pants energy that's combined with a meditative, repetitive quality that adds heft and makes 'Everybody' feel almost like a religious ritual.
Although a tad too long and obvious, Everybody is a rich theatrical experience.
Everybody, directed by Lila Neugebauer and now at Signature Theatre, is an exploration of death in our time — one that's intriguing, moving, and sometimes disappointing.
The result of what seems to be a kind of creative over-thinking, though, is that unlike the aim of its 15th century source, “Everybody” is not for everybody.
It is the most innovative aspect of this surprisingly tepid treatment of the story.
“Everybody” descends into tedium well before it ends.
What is most impressive about Everybody is that it has taken the goals of the medieval morality play and successfully translated it for the modern viewer.
I can't imagine anybody not enjoying themselves and thinking a lot about it after they've been ushered off.
An affecting and inventive new adaptation of an ancient morality play, filled with biting wit and shrewd commentary on the state of humanity.
Emerson's casual, beautifully paced performance, as well as Eno's sharp writing, make for a hypnotic duo.

It's an incredible challenge for the actors to play different parts each night but they pulled it off with such aplomb when my theatergoing buddy Bill and I saw the show that we couldn't imagine anyone other than the wonderful Lakisha Michelle May as Everybody.
Everybody is an absolute delight, which is something said of Everyman by no man ever.
But there’s no denying that Jacobs-Jenkins isn’t just anybody; he’s a playwright with a unique voice that begs listening.
“Everybody” is an entertaining production, with loads of implications about human behavior communicated by solid performances, but the play needs sharpening.
I wish I was more fully engaged with my mind and my heart, as the journey that 'Everybody' takes is huge in topic and scope, but this play just didn't feel big enough. Or deep enough.
The tale itself turns out to be unremarkable, which is disappointing.
The playwright succeeds not at being profound but at being profoundly shallow.
I am normally a fan of Brandon Jacobs-Jenkins (Gloria, An Octoroon) work, but Everybody, premiering at the Signature Theater, just left me cold.
It is unique and profound, and brilliantly achieves the purpose of the historic morality play for a modern day audience.
I definitely think you should try to see Everybody - I've not seen anything quite like it before.
There is cleverness in abundance, but I was not moved.
EVERYBODY was, alas, a disappointment.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Jacobs-Jenkins' inventive modern adaptation of the medieval morality play "Everyman." While many praise its experimental staging and humor, others find it overly self-conscious and less accessible than the playwright's previous work.
